passage: John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage
text:
The narrator says her husband John laughs at her, which she takes as an ordinary feature of marriage. The passage shows the narrator treating his mockery as a familiar, almost expected part of their relationship rather than as a serious conflict.

The sentence is a light, self-aware aside from the narrator on page 1. It sets up the document's central tension: she perceives something unusual about the house, while John dismisses her perceptions as nerves or imagination. The phrase "one expects that in marriage" signals her resigned acceptance of his doubt, which will matter later as he keeps reassuring her and she increasingly keeps her thoughts to herself. p. 1

Read in context, the line is an early hint of her isolation. Her husband's laughter is gentle on the surface but already marks a gap between how she sees her situation and how he does, a gap the story widens as her confinement and suspicion grow.

passage: I am sitting by the window now, up in this atrocious nursery
text:
The narrator is sitting by the window in the upstairs nursery, which she calls atrocious, and she is free to write as much as she likes apart from her lack of strength. The passage sits on page 3, which opens with her note that she has been in the house two weeks and had not felt like writing since the first day p. 3.

The word "atrocious" is her strong dislike of the room, a former playroom with barred windows and rings in the walls, which she finds ugly and unpleasant p. 1. Her remark that nothing hinders her writing except lack of strength matters because her husband John has forbidden her to work, so her ability to write is shaped by his rules and her illness p. 1.

passage: He says that with my imaginative power and habit of story-making
text:
The narrator says her husband John warns that, because she has a vivid imagination and likes making up stories, her nervous weakness will lead to many excited fancies.

John says that, with my imaginative power and habit of story-making, a nervous weakness like mine is sure to lead to all manner of excited fancies, and that I ought to use my will and good sense to check the tendency.

passage: send me to Weir Mitchell in the fall
text: The passage claims that John says he will send the narrator to Weir Mitchell in the fall if she does not improve, and that a friend of hers was once in Mitchell's hands and found him like John and her brother, only more so. The document offers no support for any factual claim about Mitchell; the narrator's remarks are personal impressions and are presented as her own opinion of him.

passage: Personally, I disagree with their ideas
text:
The objection: the narrator's disagreement is unsupported, since her own nervous state may distort her judgment of her treatment.

A careful critic would note that the narrator asserts "Personally, I disagree with their ideas" as if it were a sound counter-judgment, yet she admits elsewhere that her condition makes her feel bad and that she is prone to "excited fancies." Her husband and brother are physicians, and the rest cure she rejects is the standard advice of the period. A reader could reasonably conclude that her rejection is itself a symptom of the illness the men diagnose, which would weaken her claim to know what is good for her. The text on page 1 gives her only her own feelings as evidence that work would help, with no test or outcome offered to support it.

The author's best reply, as the story implies, is that the narrator's sense of being stifled is real and that the restrictions imposed on her actually deprive her of the stimulation she needs, so her disagreement is grounded in her lived experience rather than whim p. 1.

passage: I have locked the door and thrown the key down into the front path
question: Why does she throw the key away?
text:
She says why right after the action: "I don't want to go out, and I don't want to have anybody come in, till John comes" p. 12. The locked door and the discarded key guarantee that no one can interrupt her before her husband returns. The next line gives her aim: "I want to astonish him" p. 12.

The practical reason is the wallpaper. She has been working to peel it off, and on the previous page she saw Jennie try to get her out of the room, which she called "too patent" p. 11. She also insists that "no person touches this paper but me" p. 11. With the key gone, no one can stop her from finishing what she believes is freeing the woman behind the pattern.

The key also becomes a weapon in the final scene. When John pounds on the door, she calmly tells him the key is "down by the front steps, under a plantain leaf" p. 12, and repeats it until he goes to fetch it p. 13. The document doesn't comment on this, but the effect is that she controls the pacing of his entry. The same man who has dictated her every hour must now obey her instructions and wait.

From general knowledge, readers often take the discarded key as a symbolic reversal: she has been locked in a barred nursery, and now she is the one who decides who gets in and out.

Before you start
×

A woman, confined by her physician husband to a rented summer mansion for a supposed nervous condition, keeps a secret journal. Her fixation on the yellow wallpaper of her nursery room grows as the story moves through the summer.

Where we are

A couple rent a secluded colonial mansion for the summer; the narrator is forbidden to work and told to rest because of her "nervous depression." p. 1
They live in a former nursery at the top of the house, with barred windows, a bed fixed in place and peeling, repellent yellow wallpaper. p. 2
The narrator writes in secret, since her husband and his sister disapprove. The rental runs three months, so time is limited. p. 7

People

The narrator — Unnamed writer of the journal, a wife and new mother, treated as an invalid and cut off from work and company.
John — Her husband, a practical physician who dismisses her fears and directs her every hour.
Jennie — John's sister, a devoted housekeeper who looks after the household and the narrator.
Mary — The nurse who cares for the narrator's baby.
Her brother — Also a physician, who agrees with John's diagnosis of her condition.

Threads to watch

Her own sense of her illness and need for meaningful work clashes with the rest cure her husband and brother insist on. p. 1
The wallpaper's pattern, and a figure behind it, take over her attention. Watch how her account of what she sees changes. p. 7
She hides her writing, her wakefulness and her thoughts from John, while he and Jennie seem increasingly watchful of her. p. 8
The narrator's trust in John is strained as she asks to leave and is refused, with the lease ending in weeks. p. 7
